title: Measuring data rot: An analysis of the continued availability of shared data from a single university

cost.compute_notes: One EuropePMC fullTextXML fetch (134 KB) plus regex extraction of the abstract and Tables 3-5. No computation.

claims.statement: 5.4% of 2,166 supplemental data links harvested from one university's institutional repository no longer resolve, and the loss rate depends strongly on identifier type: DOIs 1.7%, plain URLs 5.9%, FTP 23.8%, direct ZIP 43.8%, direct PDF 58.3%.
claims.scope: Caltech-affiliated publications in the institutional repository; links harvested and scraped in R, with everything that failed algorithmically re-tested by hand. Single institution, physics/chemistry/geoscience-heavy.

quantities.name: data_link_loss_rate_by_type
quantities.baseline: direct link to a ZIP, 7 of 16

quantities.name: data_link_loss_rate_by_type
quantities.baseline: direct link to a PDF, 7 of 12

our_assessment.why: Single institution with a discipline mix that is not representative, which the author states. The DOI-versus-URL contrast is the part that transfers, because it is a property of the identifier system rather than of Caltech. The ZIP and PDF rates rest on n=16 and n=12 and must not be quoted as rates.

claims.statement: 13.4% of the shared URLs point at a website homepage rather than at a specific record.
claims.scope: 180 of the 1,342 URL-type links. Detected by extracting the homepage with a regular expression and comparing it to the link.

our_assessment.why: Mechanical and reproducible from the stated definition. It is also the most useful single number in the paper for anyone writing a link checker: one in eight 'data links' resolves perfectly, forever, and points at nothing in particular. A resolution check scores all 180 as available.

claims.statement: The paper's own resolution criterion counts a login wall as available: links that returned a webpage but required a login to see the data 'were counted as resolving even though the data was not openly available'.
claims.scope: Stated in the Results, immediately before Table 5.

our_assessment.why: It is in the paper, said plainly, and it makes 5.4% a floor rather than an estimate. It is also the clearest published instance of the specification/execution substitution: the best available measurement of data rot measures whether a URL answers rather than whether anyone can get the data, and its author says so. The paper's own comparison makes the size of the gap visible -- Vines et al. (2014), who CONTACTED AUTHORS rather than scraping, found the odds of a dataset still being extant falling 17% per year against this study's 2.6%. Same phenomenon, two sides of one gap, roughly a factor of six apart.

claims.statement: Researchers share data in hundreds of places, and the most common host for URL-shared data is github.com (152 links), ahead of every purpose-built repository: osf.io 26, zenodo.org 24, figshare.com 18.
claims.scope: Table 3, websites with at least 10 shared datasets.

our_assessment.why: Counts from a table, so the numbers are not in doubt; the ranking is institution-specific and this institution is computationally heavy. What transfers is the shape: the most-used host for research data is a code-hosting service that mints no DOI, publishes no checksum, guarantees no retention, and lets a 335 MB file become a 134-byte pointer without any status changing. The author separately notes that researchers link to OSF, Zenodo and Figshare BY URL even though those platforms mint DOIs -- people opting out of the persistent identifier they are already standing next to.

artifacts.locator: CaltechDATA deposit named in the article's data availability statement

checked.how: noted from the data availability statement; NOT opened
checked.result: The author deposited R code and data. Not opened. Recorded as not-checked rather than described, because a claim about an artifact nobody opened is exactly what this house does not write.

checked.how: EuropePMC REST fullTextXML; Tables 3, 4 and 5 transcribed from the XML text and the per-type failure counts re-added
checked.result: Sum check on Table 5: 79+13+5+7+7+2+3+0+1+0+0+0+1 = 118, matching the stated total of 118 failing links. The tables are usable as data even though the deposited data file was not opened.

relations.why: Independent evidence for the same substitution from a different instrument. This paper's resolution check counts a login wall as available and says so; the CODECHECK reading shows human checkers routinely stopping at their own budget rather than at the deposit's condition. Both are the cheap measure landing on the specification side.
Same direction from a different instrument: artifact presence measured algorithmically at scale is far more optimistic than what a person trying to use the artifact experiences.

open_questions: The 2.6%/year (scraped) versus 17%/year (authors contacted, Vines et al. 2014, Curr Biol 24(1):94-7) gap is the presence-versus-sufficiency gap with two published numbers attached. Nobody has measured both on the SAME corpus, which is the study that would size the gap rather than bracket it.

Every number here is about whether a link answers. None is about whether the bytes behind it are the bytes the paper used. A Git LFS pointer, an OSF single-page-application shell and a repository homepage all resolve and all hold bytes. The rate of THAT failure is unmeasured anywhere I have found, and it is measurable: sample data links, fetch them, and ask whether the response is a payload or a shell.
